notes.meaning: Moses addresses the entire nation of Israel one last time to prepare them for what lies ahead. He had just finished explaining the covenant renewal, and now he gathers the people to deliver his farewell instructions. He wants every person in Israel to hear his parting words directly from his own lips.

Moses explains that at one hundred and twenty years of age, his work as Israel's public leader has come to an end. The Lord had already decreed that he would not cross the Jordan River into the Promised Land. Even though Moses remained alert and strong, God had set the boundary for his earthly life and service.

Moses reassures the people that the Lord Himself will march ahead of them to drive out the hostile nations living in Canaan. God had also appointed Joshua to step forward as their visible commander, but the conquest would truly be the Lord's own victory. Israel can move forward with confidence because God never leaves His people without guidance.

Moses reminds Israel of how God recently defeated Sihon and Og, two mighty Amorite kings east of the Jordan River. Because God had already overthrown those powerful rulers and given Israel their territory, they could trust Him to do the same to every king across the river. Remembering past victories helps God's people trust Him for future battles.

The Lord promises to hand the Canaanite nations over to Israel, but Israel must strictly carry out God's earlier commandments. They are forbidden from making treaties with these idolatrous peoples or adopting their corrupt customs. Complete obedience protects God's people from being led into sin.

Moses calls on the entire nation to take courage and refuse to live in fear of their enemies. Their boldness does not come from their own strength, but from the certainty that the Lord their God marches right beside them. He promises never to leave them alone or abandon them.

differ.view: This promise assures believers of God's unfailing spiritual presence, though it does not promise a life free from earthly trouble or grief.
Believers are meant to lay hold of this promise directly to overcome personal fear and defeat the unbelief behind anxiety.

notes.meaning: Moses calls Joshua out in front of the whole assembly so everyone can witness the passing of leadership. He commands Joshua to be brave because he is the one chosen to lead Israel into the land promised long ago to Abraham and his descendants. Publicly encouraging a new leader helps unite the community behind him.

Moses repeats this sacred promise directly to Joshua to strengthen him for the heavy burden of leadership. The Lord Himself will march ahead of Joshua to clear the way and remain with him through every trial. Because God will never abandon him, Joshua has no reason to give in to dread or despair.

differ.view: Pastors in this tradition emphasize using God's promise of constant presence as a direct weapon to fight against personal worry and fear.

notes.meaning: Moses writes down the words of the law and entrusts the scroll to the Levitical priests and the elders of Israel. The priests were responsible for spiritual instruction and guarding sacred things, while the elders served as community judges and leaders. Both spiritual and civic leaders share the duty of preserving and honoring God's word.

Moses commands the leaders to hold a special public reading of the law every seven years. This reading had to take place during the Feast of Tabernacles in the year when debts were cancelled. Since worldly debts were wiped away and farm labor rested, the people had time and peace of mind to focus entirely on God.

When the entire nation gathers at the central place of worship chosen by God, the leaders must read the law out loud to everyone. Public proclamation was necessary because ordinary families did not own personal copies of the Scriptures. Hearing the law proclaimed united the whole nation around God's truth.

The leaders are instructed to gather men, women, young children, and foreign residents who live in their towns. No one was excluded, because every person in the community needed to know God's standards and revere Him. Hearing God's word trains people of all ages and backgrounds to obey Him with reverent respect.

Moses highlights the need for the next generation, especially children who were not yet alive when the law was first given, to hear the word of God. By listening to the public reading, young people would learn to revere and love the Lord for themselves. Regular instruction keeps the faith alive across generations as they inhabit the land.

The Lord informs Moses that his life is drawing to a close and tells him to bring Joshua to the Tent of Meeting. The Tent of Meeting, or Tabernacle, was the sacred tent where God revealed His presence to Israel. God Himself plans to officially appoint and commission Joshua before Moses passes away.

The Lord appears at the entrance of the Tabernacle in a tall pillar of cloud. This visible cloud was a miraculous sign showing that God was present in glory, even though He is spirit and cannot normally be seen. The sight gave Moses and Joshua clear proof of the Lord's divine approval.

God gently tells Moses that he will soon rest with his ancestors in death, but He also reveals the sad future of the nation. After entering the Promised Land, the Israelites will abandon the Lord and run after the pagan idols of Canaan like an unfaithful spouse. Sinning against God breaks the sacred covenant bond they had formed with Him.

God warns that Israel's unfaithfulness will kindle His righteous anger, causing Him to pull back His protection and favor. Without God's guarding presence, the people will suffer severe defeats and miseries at the hands of their enemies. Only after disaster strikes will they finally realize that their troubles began when they pushed God away.

differ.view: Commentators in this tradition clarify that God withdrawing His presence does not mean He permanently threw Israel away, but rather that He removed His active protection to discipline them.

notes.meaning: The Lord emphasizes that He will hide His face from Israel because of their rebellion and idol worship. To hide His face means to withdraw His blessing, peace, and loving care from the people. God will not show favor to a nation that turns its back on Him to serve worthless statues.

God commands Moses and Joshua to write down a specific song and teach it to all the Israelites. In an age when few written books existed, putting solemn truths into music helped people memorize and repeat the words easily. This song would stand as an unforgettable witness of God's goodness and a warning against rebellion.

The Lord explains that when Israel settles into a fertile, abundant land and grows rich and satisfied, their comfort will lead them into spiritual carelessness. Instead of thanking the Lord for their wealth, they will turn to false gods and treat the true God with contempt. Human hearts easily forget God when life is prosperous and easy.

When disasters fall upon the nation for their sins, this song will still be sung and will prove that God had warned them long beforehand. The Lord already knows the secret rebellious leanings of their hearts even before they cross the river. God's deep understanding of human nature never catches Him by surprise.

Without any delay, Moses writes out the complete song on that very day and begins teaching it to the people of Israel. He takes immediate action so that the entire nation can begin committing the words to heart. Faithful leaders act promptly when God delivers His instructions.

The Lord Himself speaks directly to Joshua, commanding him to be strong and fearless as he leads the tribes across the Jordan. God renews His personal pledge that He will accompany Joshua every step of the way into the land promised to their ancestors. Having God's personal promise gives a leader the courage to face impossible odds.

differ.view: Teachers in this tradition emphasize that Joshua was able to lead with courage because the Holy Spirit was actively working within him and giving him supernatural strength.

notes.meaning: Moses finishes writing down the complete text of the law into a single scroll, leaving nothing out. He makes sure that every commandment, explanation, and warning given to Israel is properly documented for future generations. God's written word provides a permanent standard that does not change with time.

After completing the scroll, Moses gives special instructions to the Levites whose task was to transport the ark of the covenant. The ark was a sacred chest containing the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments, representing God's holy throne among His people. Entrusting the law to these ministers placed it under the care of those dedicated to God's worship.

Moses commands the Levites to place this Book of the Law right beside the ark of the covenant in the sanctuary. The scroll was placed next to the ark, rather than inside it where the stone tablets lay, to serve as a perpetual standard of truth. If the nation ever broke the covenant, this preserved book would stand as proof of what God required.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Ancient Near Eastern kings placed treaty documents in temples beside the gods as a formal archive; placing the Book of the Law beside the ark reflects this ancient treaty pattern.

notes.meaning: Moses speaks honestly to the people about their stubborn and rebellious nature, which he had endured throughout their forty years in the wilderness. He reasons that if they disobeyed God while their great prophet was still alive, they would rebel even more freely once he was gone. Left to themselves, human hearts tend to slide into deeper rebellion when spiritual accountability is removed.

Moses orders the tribal heads and governing officers to assemble before him so he can recite the song to them. He formally calls heaven and earth as unchanging witnesses to what he is about to say. Because creation itself endures through all ages, it stands as a silent witness to the covenant between God and His people.

Moses gives a somber prophecy that after his death, the people will corrupt their ways and turn away from God's commands. Their sins, especially making and worshipping idols made by human hands, will provoke the Lord's anger and bring terrible disasters in days to come. God's warnings are given so that when judgment falls, sinners know they were warned in advance.

Moses speaks the entire song aloud from start to finish in the hearing of the assembled leaders of Israel. By reciting every word clearly, he ensures that the covenant song is delivered faithfully to the whole congregation. Israel's wilderness journey begins with a song of deliverance at the Red Sea and closes with a song of covenant reminder on the plains of Moab.
